extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers studying American government and the presidency
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style exposition of the constitutional and practical powers of the U.S. President, covering administrative direction, appointment and removal, war and military authority, foreign affairs, pardons, and the President's legislative role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to see laws, treaties, and judicial decisions faithfully executed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is his duty to see that the Constitution, laws, and treaties of the United States, and judicial decisions rendered by the federal courts are duly enforced everywhere throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This function defines the President as head of the national administration and underlies many other executive powers; it is cited as the basis for directing department heads and for use of force to enforce federal law when ordinary civil process is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to direct administrative officers (degree variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: He may direct the heads of departments and their subordinates in the discharge of the functions vested in them by the acts of Congress, though the exact degree of control is often a matter of political controversy and depends on personality and constitutional theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some departments are more directly subject to presidential control (e.g., Secretary of State in foreign affairs; Attorney-General must give opinions or institute proceedings when required), while others (historically the Treasury) were thought to be under special Congressional control. Court rulings have held the President bound to ensure faithful discharge but not to direct the precise methods of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential removal power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has the power to remove the head of a department who refuses to obey his orders and, generally, can remove officers he appoints without consulting the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Constitution is silent except for impeachment, practice has accepted removal as inherent in appointment; the Tenure of Office Act (1867) briefly required Senate consent for removals but was later modified/repealed. Federal judges remain removable only by impeachment. Historical examples: President Jackson removed Treasury secretaries to achieve his policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinance (rulemaking) power
rubrics_metrics.description: The President possesses a large ordinance power — authority to supplement statutes by rules and regulations covering matters of detail such as army and navy regulations, patent office, customs, internal revenue, consular and civil service rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules may be issued under specific statutory authority or under general executive power (commander-in-chief for military rules). The ordinance power gives the President significant administrative authority within statutory lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to direct law enforcement and use armed force
rubrics_metrics.description: As chief executive the President may instruct the Attorney-General to institute proceedings against anyone suspected of violating federal law, and in case of open resistance he may employ the armed force of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grants the President discretion over laxness or severity in enforcement. Statutory provisions also authorize use of militia/army when obstructions or insurrection make ordinary judicial enforcement impracticable (example: Cleveland's use of federal troops during the Chicago strike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and control of appointments (advice and consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil officers (other than certain specified exceptions) fall into two groups: (1) officers whose appointment is vested by the Constitution or act of Congress in the President and Senate, and (2) inferior officers whose appointment may be vested by Congress in the President, courts, or heads of departments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first group includes department heads, many bureau chiefs, inferior federal judges, commissioners, revenue officers, and postmasters in large cities. Appointment procedures and the President's freedom vary by group; Senate confirmation is required for many important posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical groups of presidential appointments (degrees of freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices filled by the President and Senate may be divided into groups according to the degree of freedom the President enjoys: (1) Cabinet and major posts usually his personal selection, (2) positions subject to senatorial courtesy and senatorial control, and (3) minor district-level positions where Representatives often recommend appointees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate usually ratifies Cabinet nominations; senatorial courtesy gives home-state Senators large influence over certain appointments; Representatives of the President's party commonly recommend local postmasters. Political obligations and circumstances shape these practices (examples: Garfield conflict with Senators; described practice of sending printed blanks to Representatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recess appointment power
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Constitution, the President may fill vacancies occurring during a recess of the Senate by granting commissions which expire at the end of the next session of that body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power allows temporary appointments without immediate Senate confirmation; commissions granted in recess expire at the end of the Senate's next session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of war powers and commander-in-chief authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is commander-in-chief of the army and navy and of the state militia when called into the service of the United States, holding this power in peace as well as war; Congress, however, declares war and provides and maintains the armed forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate exists on how far Congress may direct actual operations. The President may exercise broad wartime powers (examples: Lincoln's suspension of habeas corpus, emancipation actions, blockade of ports) and may do whatever is warranted under laws of war to weaken an enemy, including governing conquered territory until Congress acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and exercises of military authority in peacetime
rubrics_metrics.description: In time of peace military officers are removed by court-martial procedures rather than at will, and the President's military authority is balanced by Congressional powers over equipment and declarations of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes ambiguity about congressional authority to countermand particular military orders, but emphasizes the President's role in the actual command of forces under constitutional framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of armed forces to enforce federal law and protect states
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may use armed forces in carrying into execution the federal law against resistance that cannot be overcome by ordinary civil process and may call forth the militia to aid states on application of state authorities or when obstructive violence makes enforcement impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory law authorizes calling militia/army when obstructions, assemblages, or rebellion prevent enforcement by ordinary judicial procedure; guaranteed to protect states against invasion and domestic violence (example: Cleveland at Chicago).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign affairs responsibilities and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is the official spokesman in conduct of foreign affairs and is primarily responsible for foreign policy, but is controlled in some matters by the Senate (treaties, confirmations) and in others by Congress (creation of diplomatic positions and funding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional powers: appoint ambassadors/ public ministers/consuls (with Senate confirmation), make treaties with two-thirds Senate consent, receive ambassadors. Congress cannot independently establish or conduct relations with foreign powers. Presidential actions in foreign affairs can have major consequences (examples: recognition of Panama by Roosevelt; sending ships like the Maine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and provocative acts in foreign relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's power to receive foreign representatives authorizes him to recognize the independence of new states and to dismiss foreign ministers; he may order fleets or ships abroad in ways that can provoke international difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts may embroil the country in war or diplomatic crises; historical examples include Polk's actions in the Mexican War and McKinley's deployment of the Maine to Havana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive agreements (making international arrangements without Senate consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President may make 'executive agreements' with foreign powers without the consent of the Senate; not all international arrangements are 'treaties' requiring Senate ratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The line between treaty and executive agreement is difficult to draw. Presidents have implemented treaty-like policies via executive agreements when the Senate refused to ratify treaties (example: Roosevelt's Santo Domingo actions after Senate rejection). This power can allow substantial international commitments without formal Senate approval and has been criticized as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to grant reprieves and pardons
rubrics_metrics.description: The President enjoys the power to grant reprieves and pardons (except in cases of impeachment) for offenses against the United States; no limits are imposed and pardons may be granted before, during, or after trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President may remit fines, commute sentences, or free an offender but cannot restore forfeiture of office. The clemency process typically runs through the Attorney-General's office (pardon-clerk) with input from judges and district attorneys; Presidents generally rely on these opinions when deciding (example: Harrison's statement on deference to trial courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: The President's legislative functions (informing and recommending)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is required to give Congress information on the state of the Union and to recommend measures he judges necessary and expedient; he may recommend laws and even draw bills which Congress may accept, modify, or reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presidential message (e.g., State of the Union) is widely read and influential in public opinion and congressional action. Story is cited arguing the executive's unique informational advantage on domestic and foreign matters, justifying the requirement that the President lay facts and recommendations before Congress.
